newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends with steep gains on temp forecast.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends with steep gains on temp forecast.

text.p: NYMEX crude and heating oil rocketed to a sharply higher finish as forecasts of a prolonged cold spell in many U.S. regions threatened tight supplies of heating oil, traders said.
"The market is anticipating a cold snap, and maybe two snaps behind that one," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc.

January crude settled up $1.27 a barrel at $25.74. Prompt crude hit a contract high intraday of $25.95, just shy of crude's post-Gulf War high of $26.10 hit October 22. January heating oil finished up 3.11 cents a gallon at 74.82 cents.
Spot heat also hit a contract high intraday of 75.70 cents. The post-Gulf War high for heat is 76.75 cents made on October 8.

"There were plenty of stops hit after $25.60," said a New York crude trader, explaining crude's gains were sharpened by technical buy programs. Jan gasoline ended up 2.48 cents a gallon at 69.52 cents in sympathy with the oil complex.

Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said an artic air mass from Siberia would create much below normal temperatures in the U.S. Midwest by midweek and in the Northeast by the weekend. He said the cold spell may last through year-end.
Weather Services Corp said bouts of below normal temperatures in Northeast and Midwest could last through the first half of January.
The American Petroleum Institute said at December 6 heating oil stocks were 12.6 million barrels below year ago. Traders said refiners have been meeting demand through high output.
"Heating oil had been the most oversold commodity of the group. We could test the (post-Gulf War) highs from here," said Kevelson.
Dealers said a prolonged cold spell could result in heating oil demand outstripping refiner production, leaving low stocks as the only buffer to shortage.
"We have been bearly keeping above water with high refiner runs. The inventory situation is still very bullish," said GSC Energy trader Al Lindseth.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
